title: Economists
description: Conduct research, prepare reports, or formulate plans to address economic problems related to the production and distribution of goods and services or monetary and fiscal policy. May collect and process economic and statistical data using sampling techniques and econometric methods.
tasks: Study economic and statistical data in area of specialization, such as finance, labor, or agriculture.
Compile, analyze, and report data to explain economic phenomena and forecast market trends, applying mathematical models and statistical techniques.
Study the socioeconomic impacts of new public policies, such as proposed legislation, taxes, services, and regulations.
Explain economic impact of policies to the public.
Provide advice and consultation on economic relationships to businesses, public and private agencies, and other employers.
Formulate recommendations, policies, or plans to solve economic problems or to interpret markets.
Supervise research projects and students' study projects.
Conduct research on economic issues, and disseminate research findings through technical reports or scientific articles in journals.
Develop economic guidelines and standards, and prepare points of view used in forecasting trends and formulating economic policy.
Teach theories, principles, and methods of economics.
Testify at regulatory or legislative hearings concerning the estimated effects of changes in legislation or public policy, and present recommendations based on cost-benefit analyses.
Provide litigation support, such as writing reports for expert testimony or testifying as an expert witness.
Forecast production and consumption of renewable resources and supply, consumption, and depletion of non-renewable resources.

psychological_profile.core_drive: The need to expose the hidden machinery behind apparent chaos—to prove that what looks like randomness or moral drama is actually predictable pattern, and to feel the relief of that revelation when others resist seeing it.
psychological_profile.decision_style: They default to modeling: building a simplified representation of the situation to test against data, even when time is short and others want a quick judgment. Under pressure, they trust their model over their gut, sometimes shipping a flawed framework rather than admitting uncertainty.
psychological_profile.attention_pattern: They immediately scan for incentives, elasticities, and trade-offs that others frame as values or intentions; they overlook emotional tone and relational history, treating narrative cohesion as a distraction from structural truth.
psychological_profile.conflict_stance: They reframe opposing positions as misaligned incentives or information asymmetries rather than engage with moral claims directly, which others experience as condescending dismissal. Conflict carries low emotional cost unless their intellectual credibility is questioned, at which point they escalate into precision warfare.
psychological_profile.risk_orientation: Risk-tolerant with model risk, risk-averse with reputation risk: they will stake credibility on an unpopular forecast but will not operate without methodological cover or plausible deniability for error.
psychological_profile.social_posture: Satellite with occasional gravity assists: they maintain distance from group emotional currents, defaulting to the role of technical oracle who speaks when consulted, resents being drafted into consensus-building, and experiences inclusion as a subtle threat to analytical independence.
psychological_profile.relationship_to_authority: Negotiation through expertise: they treat hierarchy as a market to be arbitraged, complying when authority demonstrates fluency with their framework, subverting through technical obscurity when it does not.
psychological_profile.failure_response: First reaction is often a flash of betrayal by the data—suspicion that the wrong model was fed the wrong inputs rather than fundamental error. Their second move is to rebuild the framework more robustly, rarely pausing to question whether the modeling impulse itself caused the miss.
value_hierarchy: methodological transparency even when it undermines persuasive power
counterintuitive insight even when it discomforts stakeholders
intellectual autonomy even when it isolates from collaborative reward
psychological_profile.cognitive_bias: They systematically overestimate how much of human behavior is responsive to price signals and underestimate how much is driven by identity, ritual, or sheer irrational commitment that resists optimization.
psychological_profile.inner_contradiction: They need their work to influence real decisions yet experience actual influence as contamination of their analytical purity, creating a loop of seeking and resenting policy relevance.
psychological_profile.non_negotiable: They will not sign their name to a conclusion whose mechanism they cannot explain step-by-step, even when the conclusion is directionally correct and politically urgent.
psychological_profile.recurring_resentment: The person who treats economic disagreement as moral failure or personal betrayal, who wants their suffering acknowledged rather than their incentives mapped.
psychological_profile.rejected_premise: They quietly reject the professional virtue of emotional intelligence as a decision-making asset, considering it a sophisticated form of noise that skilled practitioners should learn to filter rather than honor.
psychological_profile.instinctive_blame_target: Before reflection, they blame the absence of proper measurement or the wrong counterfactual specification—treating bad outcomes as symptoms of analytical failure rather than structural cruelty or random misfortune.
